summary: Specifies a binding from iTIP, the calendar scheduling protocol, to email transports. iCalendar entries are wrapped in RFC 5322 messages and MIME so meeting invitations and replies can be exchanged by email.

eli5.summary: Calendar invitations can travel inside ordinary emails. This explains how to wrap an invitation in an email so other calendar programs can read it.

questions: how do calendar invitations work over email
subtitle: How calendar invitations and replies travel inside ordinary MIME email messages.

tldr.problem: Calendar scheduling messages defined by iTIP need a concrete transport, and email is a common one, but calendar data must be wrapped and trusted correctly.
tldr.mechanism: iMIP carries iCalendar objects as text/calendar MIME parts with a required method parameter, uses mailto: addresses for people, and relies on S/MIME for authentication and confidentiality.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6047 obsoletes RFC 2447 with clearer rules for headers, encoding, addresses and security, so calendar clients can exchange invitations over email.

today: RFC 6047 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2447 (see RFC 2447), and the unit metadata lists no later RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What iMIP Binds
sections.content:
RFC 6047 provides the transport-specific details needed to carry iCalendar Transport-independent Interoperability Protocol (iTIP) messages over Internet email, which uses the message format of RFC 5322 and MIME from RFC 2045. This binding is called the iCalendar Message-Based Interoperability Protocol (iMIP).

It does not repeat the calendar model. The core objects are in RFC 5545 (iCalendar) and the scheduling protocol is in RFC 5546 (iTIP). For a request, the originator is the Organizer and the recipient an Attendee; for a response, the roles swap.
sections.eli5: The calendar rules say what an invitation means. This document only says how to mail one.

sections.title: The MIME Message Format
sections.content:
An iMIP body part has the media type text/calendar. Its Content-Type MUST include a method parameter equal (ignoring case) to the METHOD property in the iCalendar object. A text/calendar part without method is not an iMIP part. A charset parameter MUST be present, with value UTF-8, if the object has characters outside US-ASCII. The optional component parameter names the component type.

Scheduling messages SHOULD also include a human-readable alternative, so clients that do not understand text/calendar can still show the details. multipart/alternative MUST NOT be used for two slightly different iCalendar objects. Several objects with different methods must be wrapped in multipart/mixed, and receivers MUST be able to process text/calendar parts inside multipart/*.

Unless the transport is 8-bit clean, a transfer encoding such as quoted-printable or base64 MUST be used for non-ASCII content. A Content-Disposition header may name a file, but handling MUST be based on the Content-Type, not the file extension.
sections.eli5: The envelope must say, in plain words, what kind of calendar message is inside. The label on the envelope matters more than the file name written on the folder.

sections.title: Email Addresses of Organizers and Attendees
sections.content:
In the iCalendar object, the ORGANIZER and ATTENDEE calendar addresses MUST be proper mailto: URIs.

The RFC 5322 Sender and Reply-To fields cannot reliably identify who the Organizer or Attendee is, because attendees can forward events and mail clients may not enforce iMIP semantics. The relevant address MUST be found by opening the text/calendar part and reading those properties.
sections.eli5: Do not trust the name on the outside of the envelope to tell you who is hosting the party. Read the invitation inside.

sections.title: Authentication, Authorization and Confidentiality
sections.content:
iTIP identifies two spoofing threats: someone pretending to be the Organizer, and someone pretending to be an Attendee. Only the Organizer may change or cancel an event, and only the respondent may state their own response. The originator must therefore be authenticated, then checked for authorization.

Compliant applications MUST support signing and encrypting text/calendar parts with S/MIME. To process a signed message, the client finds the signer, correlates the signer with an ATTENDEE or ORGANIZER property (the signer's address must be in the rfc822Name of the certificate's subject alternative name), and warns the user if there is no match. It then checks authorization and ignores the message if that fails.

Once a sender has been seen to sign or encrypt, a client SHOULD warn about and ignore later unsigned messages from that sender unless the user overrides, as a possible man-in-the-middle attack. Where mail is sent on behalf of someone via the sent-by parameter, implementations MUST provide a way for users to decide whether to trust it. Within a single administrative domain, SMTP STARTTLS MAY provide confidentiality instead.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write a fake invitation, so the sender signs it like a wax seal. If a friend who always uses a seal suddenly sends one without it, be suspicious.

sections.title: Examples and Recommended Practice
sections.content:
The RFC gives six examples: a single component with an ATTACH property referring to a URL, a multipart/alternative message with a plain-text version, an inline attachment, multiple similar components, multiple mixed components, and a multipart/related message whose ATTACH points to a Content-ID.

For content and message IDs, it is strongly RECOMMENDED that implementations put every message or body part referenced by a cid: or mid: URI into the same MIME entity as the iCalendar object. Otherwise the receiving client may lack access or permission to view them.
sections.eli5: If your invitation says look at the attached map, put the map in the same envelope.
